Building on the success of this technology with texts from fields like law and medicine, researchers are developing novel approaches for the classification of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) texts, which often contain complex mathematical content. In this study, initial work is presented on incorporating Mathematical Entity Linking to enhance the understanding of STEM text classification, a process that involves identifying and annotating key entities within these texts, including both their names and standardized descriptions, derived from a database of commonly cited scientific publications. By integrating this Linking technology, STEM text classification becomes more transparent, revealing the specific subjects and entities these machines rely on in classifying particular documents.

To guarantee matching among all agents, the Deferred Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that stable matchings are achieved even with shorter, albeit incomplete, preference lists, thus sparking curiosity as to why and how agents should optimize these lists for the best possible matches. Researchers have explored this question in a theoretical model introduced by Lee (2016), in which preferences stem from both publicly available and private evaluations. By leveraging these shared rankings, agents can make more informed decisions when choosing which proposals to pursue. Our investigation delves into this pre-matching decision process within the algorithms driving the postgraduate job market and college admissions, ultimately showing that when rankings are easily accessible, a strategy involving short, dynamically-structured preference lists can ensure a stable matching, by prioritizing the most valuable interactions and gradually building relationships up to a matching. Furthermore, by leveraging coarse initial rankings that only distinguish between top and bottom rankings, an agent can successfully achieve a stable matching in both the medical residency market and college admissions, even when preferences are derived from mechanisms such as Chinese Auctions, by implementing a strategy Informed Choice, which allows agents to make informed decisions throughout the matching process by prioritizing interactions based on their priority ranking and choose proposals accordingly.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they are
highly unreliable in assessing human quality and limit the variety of generated
summaries. To overcome these challenges, a novel evaluation metric called
SummScore has been developed. This innovative approach utilizes a CrossEncoder
to compare the semantic meaning of original text and summaries, thus preventing
the bias against diverse summary formats. The Cross-Encoder, pre-trained on
text-matching tasks, effectively captures nuanced semantic differences between
summaries. To improve scalability, the sensitive assessment is restricted to
representative summaries and a smaller sampling of input text. Experimental
results demonstrate that SummScore correlates more strongly with human judgment
than existing evaluation metrics. Furthermore, a more advanced version of SummScore
has been created to quantify improvement in summarization models.

A new method for extracting a sparse signal from cross-related data is presented. This type of correlation is common in fields such as optics and seismic analysis, but the additional dimension creates an inverse problem bottleneck as the number of variables quadratically increases. Our solution simplifies this by only solving for the diagonal of the signal matrix, where variables increase linearly. This is made possible through a specialized "noise absorber" that filters data that does not provide signal information. This results in a linear solution at a similar cost to linear measurements. Our theoretical findings confirm exact signal recovery under clean data conditions, with zero false positives even at noisy levels, as well as an improved signal recovery rate proportional to the number of data points. Numerical simulations validate our claims.

The conventional approach to 3D object detection, where camera and LiDAR data are combined, is no longer tenable in realistic scenarios due to its vulnerability to LiDAR malfunctions. This has restricted the use of these models in practical autonomous driving applications. Our novel fusion method, called BEVFusion, stands out by not requiring any input from the LiDAR data, thereby addressing this limitation. Our results demonstrate that our method not only surpasses current standards in regular scenarios, but it also outperforms them significantly in environments that mimic real-world LiDAR malfunctions. Specifically, our method shows a substantial gain of 15.7% to 28.9% in terms of mAP when compared to existing solutions. To date, our method remains the first of its kind to tackle real-world LiDAR malfunctions effectively. The code supporting this work is available at https://github.com/ADLab-AutoDrive/BEVFusion.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted in the 1950s, thermal fluctuations have a substantial impact when the correlation scale exceeds a certain threshold relative to the dissipation scale, specifically when the Reynolds number is substantial. We verified this by calculating the correlation scale using the direct simulation of a high-Reynolds number turbulent flow and established that its value can be represented as a function of the local Reynolds number and a constant, supported by observations in various turbulent flows with different Reynolds numbers. This enabled the development of an expression for the local kinematic viscosity in terms of the Reynolds number and a fraction representing the influence of thermal fluctuations. Consequently, we propose a modified concept of Reynolds number based on the effective Reynolds number and a corrected viscosity that accounts for the effects of thermal fluctuations.

Previous studies on laser propagation through a heated fluid employed simplified thermal conductivity and convective heat transfer assumptions, leading to inaccurate predictions. This study presents an in-depth numerical analysis that accurately simulates the thermal behavior of the fluid and its impact on laser interactions. The study examines the diffracted beam in the far field produced by a laser entering the fluid, as well as the interferometric pattern formed perpendicular to the laser propagation axis. The results are validated against experimental findings, providing comprehensive insight into laser energy transfer and propagation through the fluid. The study observes and elucidates the spatial self-phase modulation and laser propagation control that can be achieved, including the observation of multiple-hump diffraction patterns.

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that existing methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions on various discussion types and projects. We introduce and demonstrate the efficacy of two techniques - data enrichment and project adaptation - to enhance the consistency of design mining outcomes across different datasets, resulting in improved performance for three datasets and increased accuracy on a test dataset.

This paper introduces a novel language called H-STREAM, specifically designed to facilitate the creation of big data pipelines that combine streaming and data history queries. H-STREAM is comprised of three key components - stream processing operators, a syntax for composing these operators, and a language-defined data type system. We focus on the design of H-STREAM's language features and propose a set of operators, querying constructs, and data types. Furthermore, we outline the specifics of its evaluation, specifically dealing with how to execute each query and how to manage different computing resources. We also detail the current implementation of an H-STREAM prototype and discuss possible applications and future areas of research, including integrating it with existing big data frameworks such as Flink and HBase.

The hunt for top and bottom companions is a critical area of study for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as their single production offers substantial detection possibilities. Though past research focused on the resonant production mode of these hypothetical particles, new findings have uncovered a diverse and complex phenomenology associated with non-resonant diagrams at leading order, particularly in the single production of top and bottom companions through vector boson fusion and associated production with vector bosons or Higgs bosons. To inform experimental searches and theoretical analyses, this paper presents a thorough examination of non-resonant diagrams, including numerical calculations, and offers recommendations for improved searches.

A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating SPARQL query generation, but these models have a major limitation: they can only handle queries based on knowledge that was learned during training. When encountering questions about new knowledge resources, classes, or properties, these models fall short, making them ineffective for handling diverse and ever-changing knowledge bases. To address this, we've developed an innovative approach that involves incorporating a mechanism to copy elements from questions directly into SPARQL questions. Experiments conducted using the T-Base dataset have revealed substantial gains, with trained models now accurately translating SPARQL questions with much greater precision and lower error rates compared to their baseline counterparts.

This work introduces a novel method for systematically categorizing and assessing the quality of diverse publishing outlets in Computer Science. Leveraging a substantial subset of the extensive DBLP dataset covering over five decades, our technique evaluates millions of contributors and thousands of publishing venues based solely on available paper publication information. By treating authorship patterns at individual publishing venues as a predictive task and focusing on key performance metrics, our method generates high-accuracy quality scores for every recorded conference and journal. Furthermore, our scores can also be utilized to model and track shifts in field dynamics across different periods. In addition, our scores can serve as a basis for evaluating both individual researchers and academic institutions, demonstrating quantitative evaluations equivalent to those derived from citation analysis or peer review processes. In contrast to many prevailing evaluation methods, our solution is both straightforward and efficient to implement. In effect, our work represents a significant advancement in the field of alternative publication metrics, often referred to as 'altmetrics.' In particular, our approach shares close affinities with the use of network analysis, being an extension of the extensive work in this field. As such, it is well-suited for the timely, automatic evaluation of the quality of individual publishing outlets. In effect, our solution represents a significant advancement in the field of alternative publication metrics, often referred to as 'altmetrics.' In particular, it differs from the prevailing use of citation analysis, focusing instead on the evaluation of the quality of individual publishing venues as a whole.

Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant analysis difficulties regarding the safety of control systems. Fortunately, recent research has introduced methods for analyzing and verifying the complex control systems. This tutorial synthesizes and introduces techniques for verifying the robustness of neural networks that originated in related fields. These techniques are further applied to establish guarantees for systems that combine neural networks and control feedback loops. Ultimately, these tools facilitate the analysis of safe control systems and support deep reinforcement learning with robustness guarantees.

This study builds upon three separate lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering and extends them in a unified manner. Specifically, we develop on the concept of functorial clustering, which was introduced by Voronoi-based functorial clustering, incorporating overlaps. This involves generalising the idea of functorial clustering to the metric space, while allowing for the possibility of empty balls and incorporating topological properties. Furthermore, we establish relationships between these novel concepts by generalising the Necessity Principle, connecting them with the continuous Massey vanishing theorem.

Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streaming video, missing tensor entries need to be recovered in real-time without compromising performance. Existing streaming completion methods may not be effective when the underlying data structure changes over time, particularly with missing data present. The approaches we discuss here: 1) use patch tracking for streaming tensor ring completion, incorporating the Warped Image Matching algorithm for better alignment of non-overlapping patches, leveraging the Warping Error to indicate the effectiveness of the warping process; 2) introduce a new framework that integrates streaming completion and patch Warping, demonstrating its superiority through theoretical analysis and empirical testing on real-world datasets.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the conjugacy classes of classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$ and $W(D_{n})$ take the form of type D. This finding has implications for the Nichols algebras associated with irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules over the classical Weyl groups $\mathbb W_{n}$, showing that these algebras have infinite dimensions, with the exception of three distinct cases: the $(2, 3),(1^{2}, 3)$ case in $\mathbb S_{5}$, and the $(1^{n-2}, 2)$ case in $\mathbb S_{n}$ for $n >5$.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed the presence of inertial wave turbulence, characterized by an unusual spectrum of kinetic and total energy. Notably, the study provided the first numerical evidence of a power-law relationship between energy fluctuations and wavenumber, with an exponent of -5/3, consistent with predictions of wave turbulence theory.

We investigate a basic model called Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN) for effectively transforming graph representations. Our analysis demonstrates that on real-valued valued graphs, IGN converges to a steady state and can replicate the behavior of the maximum weight independent set (MWIS) problem on weight matrices. However, on integer-valued graphs, GN may not converge, and we provide theoretical and empirical evidence to support the claim that GN can serve as an efficient solution method for the MWIS problem.

This research focuses on the effect of a magnetic field on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, which incorporates a series of hollows and protrusions, at low temperatures. We examine how the magnetic field influences the density of states and specific heat of this material. Our calculations show that the presence of a magnetic field significantly impacts the density of states and specific heat of electrically modulated single-layer graphene, which exhibits both unique and overlapping characteristics with those of electrically modulated single-layer graphene. For certain parameters, the material displays a combination of Landau levels and oscillating transitions between different bands. Conversely, in other scenarios, the magnetic transport characteristics resemble those of electrically modulated double-layer graphene. Furthermore, the study reveals that the electronic band gap in electrically modulated single-layer graphene can be adjusted by applying a magnetic field. According to the results, the magnetic field induces two distinct transitions in the material: a recombination transition, which reduces the number of bands at high magnetic fields, and a multiple-band transition, which forms new bands at low magnetic fields. The study also shows that the presence of a magnetic field influences the relative positions of electrically modulated single-layer graphene and electrically modulated double-layer graphene. For certain parameters, the material displays a combination of Landau levels and oscillating transitions between different bands. In addition to these unique properties, the study of electrically modulated single-layer graphene also shows that the magnetic transport characteristics resemble those of electrically modulated double-layer

Recent findings have identified low-frequency radio emission from systems consisting of small cool stars called M dwarfs, which shares similar patterns to magnetospheric phenomena observed in our Solar System. The radio emission could be triggered by a star's magnetic field or rotative interaction with any companion stars, mainly observed in binary systems. Our research monitored the star systems CR Draconis, a binary system consisting of two M dwarfs, over a long period of time using a wideband driver for a radio telescope. Our data revealed significant low-frequency radio emission continuing for around 350 days with repeated patterns of about 9.5 days, also present were higher frequency superimposed emission possibly triggered by the interaction of the two stars in the binary system. The emission levels significantly dropped when observing the less active star of the binary system, however when observing the more active star the emission levels showed large fluctuations. The patterns and levels of the radio emission from the more active star did not match expected patterns from the rotation of the star or a long-term stable loop of magnetic field, however remained consistent with the presence of a persistent electron-cyclotron maser emission driven by the magnetic field of the star.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges for realistic virtual
human avatars, we developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new framework that
extends DNR. In experiments and user evaluations, ANR consistently outperformed DNR
and other baseline methods on various aspects of visual quality, leading the field
in a more competitive space.

Artificial intelligence experts have relied on automated methods, particularly eye-tracking and classification experiments, to evaluate how humans interpret images. However, these techniques might not accurately reflect human visual perception since they rely on the same mathematical transformations as machine models. To investigate the impact of image manipulations on human performance, we've created a novel, mathematically pure experimental setup where manipulated images are evaluated by human participants alongside their machine counterparts. Our analysis of this controlled environment reveals that certain image processing techniques, like zooming or rotating, have no effect on human performance, whereas others, such as reversing image coordinates, significantly lower it. Notably, we've found that Reversed Flipped (RF) images challenge both humans and machines, with little distinction observed in performance. Although RF transformations are applied uniformly, they produce diverse outcomes in image classification, and we explain this observation through the lens of optimal geometric embedding principles.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory, along with its relationship to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant, which uses quantum algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{su}_2)$, is examined in this exploration. Certain tangle diagrams associated with three strands that include a spin-$1/2$ closed loop demonstrate a connection to the AW algebra's generators. Both the Chern-Simons theory and the Reshetikhin-Turaev construction show that the link invariants generated by these tangles adhere to the algebra's generator relationships. This reveals that the Chern-Simons theory's expectation values for Wilson loops satisfy AW algebra relations and the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariants fail to differentiate between equivalent linear combinations of links.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which effectively tackles the thermodynamic properties of frustrated two-dimensional materials composed of connected triangular (PT) and kagome (KT) lattices. Specifically, our research focused on the low-temperature behavior of an almost decoupled PT-KT lattice and the effects of its underlying symmetry on the observed spin properties, particularly in the presence of weak interlayer coupling. Furthermore, our analysis examined the influence of different structural elements, such as hexagons and seven-bonded unit cells, on the symmetry and nature of the order parameters present in the system. Additionally, we investigated the presence of zero-temperature phase transitions and compared our results with those from a mean-field analysis focusing on a decoupled PT layer.

Pre-trained language models have shown impressive performance across various tasks when fine-tuned with relevant data and carefully crafted prompts. However, obtaining this prompt and dataset information is often costly and time-consuming. Our study focuses on developing an adaptable system that uses meta-learning to streamline the process of zero-shot learning for any given task by optimizing model parameters with a large dataset and prompt collection. This goal is achieved through the systematic design of a comprehensive dataset collection of 21 diverse datasets, 85 prompts sets, and over 220,000 examples that showcase a wide range of tasks and characteristics. Our proposed approach relies on the Transformer and ALBERT models to create a unified framework that can adapt model parameters to unseen tasks while promoting transfer learning, diversity, and data utility. Evaluations across 21 datasets, covering 8 distinct tasks, demonstrate that our method surpasses strong baselines, with notable gains of 11.2% and 6.9% in average performance in a zero-shot and few-shot setting respectively.

In depth research into the likelihood and characteristics of a robust first-order electroweak phase transition has been carried out as a prerequisite to studying electroweak baryogenesis within the context of the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM, considering recent data from the Higgs sector, numerous benchmark scenarios, and various numerical simulations involving Fréchet derivatives for beyond the SM contributions to the effective potential. The results indicate that certain groups of our previously found NMSSM benchmarks meet the requirements for successful electroweak baryogenesis, with the most stringent constraints derived from Higgs decays into $b\bar b$ and the LHC searches for the mass of the Higgs boson. The analysis also assesses the potential for detection of stochastic gravitational waves generated by the phase transition, prioritizing a broad frequency range. The experiments that will likely conduct this search, DECIGO and LISA, have been considered. Finally, using the principle of energy conservation, we have extended the calculation of the bounce action and evaluated its related concepts (such as the phase transition strength, the duration factor, and latent heat) in addition to the previously employed energy barrier and curvatures in the potential. The influence of these factors on the detection prospects have been examined and their implications explained.

We introduce novel approaches for visually identifying reliable redshifts through emission lines in the millimeter and submillimeter spectrum. Our methodology involves evaluating the effectiveness of diverse millimeter and submillimeter observational methods in measuring spectroscopic redshifts and optimizes future observations to maximize the proportion of robust redshifts. To facilitate this process, a publicly accessible code is shared at (https://github.com/cecilehajnal/Redshift-pulling-data/tree/compressed- reddi). We discuss how our methods complement other redshift measurement techniques and highlight their implications for future redshift surveys, particularly those using ground-based and space-based telescopes operating in the millimeter range.

This research uses large-scale matrix-product state simulations to determine the dynamical spin structure factor of the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice with antiferromagnetic properties. A highly complex phase diagram arises from the lattice due to the conflicting interactions of adjacent and diagonal spins. Where the former favors antiferromagnetic ordering and the latter promotes a spin liquid, although actual ground states exhibit complex behavior. Our results confirm that the spin liquid exhibits no signature in the magnetic momentum spectrum. Moreover, we identify the 120-degree antiferromagnetic and the extended $Z_3$ ordered phases through the analysis of the magnetic form factors. However, the $Z_2 \times Z_2$ ordered phase, which is created by the extended $Z_3$ phase, leaves its mark in the magnetic form factors and the dynamical spin structure factor, particularly in the nearest neighbor spin correlations. The latter property is similar to that of the spin liquid and the 120-degree antiferromagnetic phase, thus we conclude that the nearest neighbor spin correlations alone are insufficient for differentiating these three phases. The ground states of the model exhibit a phase separation between the 120-degree and the extended $Z_3$ phases along a specific tension trail. A ground state that is three-fold degenerate arises from the latter phase when it is stabilized. The effect of the neighboring spin interaction on the dynamical spin structure factor is examined, along with the spin-lattice

The study explores lattice cutoff effects on the phase transition in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory across four dimensions and their implications on $Z_3$ symmetry, where a complex triplet Higgs boson has no initial mass and interaction. Through generalized polyhedral domain methods, the investigation simulates lattice systems generating gauge field configurations based on $Z_3$ symmetry, thereby monitoring the deconfinement transition in 4D $SU(3)-$Higgs theory. Analyzing the behavior of the lowest eigenvalue spectrum of the transfer matrix, the research derives the latent heat associated with the deconfinement transition and compares it with numerical results obtained from Monte Carlo simulations.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal structure similar to Mn$_2$Au and is of interest in the study of antiferromagnetic spintronics due to its in-plane N\'{e}el vector degeneracy. This study focuses on growing Cr$_2$Al crystals and examining its magnetic properties as a function of orientation. Using neutron diffraction and simulations, the research finds that Cr$_2$Al has a magnetic ordering identical to Mn$_2$Au and is likely to provide new insights into spintronics through comparison with Mn$_2$Au. The results also validate the assumptions behind theoretical models of Mn$_2$Au and explain the observations of previous studies on amorphous and powder forms of Cr$_2$Al.

A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. By integrating relaxation-time approximation, the $
u$-model's collision frequency becomes velocity-dependent, incorporating essential collision characteristics from Boltzmann's equation, while also reflecting the influence of the target velocity distribution function, akin to the Shakhov model. Following numerical simulations of rarefied gas flows with both model gases and polyatomic gases, comparable results to those obtained from the model-free Monte-Carlo method or Shakhov model were obtained. Additionally, the $
u$-model has performance advantages over Shakhov model as it is computationally more stable and permits the use of time-explicit spatially-implicit numerical schemes.

Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge in NLP. The latest state-of-the-art semantic parsers employ sequence-to-sequence models, built upon vast language datasets, yet these models fall short in delivering practical applications due to their limited handling of unknown words and complex structures. To address this limitation, we introduce Naturalized Semantic Parser (NSP), a groundbreaking parser that leverages multiple cutting-edge techniques for improved performance, including the use of multilingual pre-trained models, word embeddings derived from operational data, and efficient handling of unknown words and complex sentences. Evaluation across 8 datasets, including a newly created dataset for access control, demonstrates NSP's superior accuracy, with an average increase of 11% over the previous best results, utilizing only 5% of the data required for constant computational resources, a significant achievement in delivering practical applications of semantic parsing.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. To determine crucial information, precise measurements of heavy quarks formed in these collisions are vital. To obtain this information, cutting-edge forward detectors must provide accurate data. Design work for one such forward detector, the Forward Silicon Tracker, is in progress, focusing on employing advanced silicon technologies. This detector is crucial in identifying heavy quarks, gathering crucial information about their formation processes, and analyzing their properties. Utilizing advanced silicon technologies, this detector will be capable of capturing precise data on collision events, thereby enhancing our understanding of matter's fundamental components.

A new discovery in X-ray variability patterns in four galaxies, identified as Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs), has led researchers to re-evaluate the case of the low-mass Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) 2XMM J123103.2+110648 as a potential QPE host galaxy. By analyzing archived XMM-Newton data and applying the autocorrelation function, scientists found variability timescales of 13.52 and 14.35 thousand seconds for the AGN in question. Furthermore, the results suggested that one of the timescales was possibly affected by a count rate that was twice as high as expected. In an attempt to examine the nature of the observed variability patterns, the researchers tested multiple models such as a stably accreting supermassive Black Hole, a reverberation delay, a stalling/Unstable Accretion Disk, and a Quasi-Periodic Eruption. Ultimately, the results indicated a 68% likelihood that the observed variability was caused by Quasi-Periodic Eruption, a 21% possibility that it was affected by a reverberation delay, and a 12% possibility that it was caused by a stalling/Unstable Accretion Disk, with a significant uncertainty in all scenarios.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long sparked debate about their influence on the atmospheres of stars. Our research provides new evidence from spectropolarimetric analysis on how the strength of a magnetic field in HD58260, a magnetic star, decreases as you move higher in its atmosphere. The results suggest that the outer atmosphere has a magnetic field roughly one-third as strong as its inner layers. The increased flow of high-energy particles in magnetic fields near these stars may explain their surrounding magnetospheres and the surrounding bow shocks that form due to the interaction between the star's magnetic field and the surrounding space.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) and assess the reliability of other SFR measurement techniques. By assuming that the galaxy's interstellar medium is in thermal equilibrium with the gas temperatures (T$_{dust}$ = 32 K), we derived a SFR = 0.035 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$. Utilizing the galaxy's CO and H30α flux ratios, we obtained SFR values of 0.022 and 0.030 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, respectively. These SFR values are in line with previous estimates based on UV and IR data. However, our H30α-derived SFR is 30% higher than the CO-based value, and notably, our H30α SFR is 40% lower than the UV+IR-based value, with the CO and H30α SFR values being 15% and 25% off respectively. We found the ratio of CO to H30α flux to be 0.06, with the ratio of UV to H30α flux being 3.5, and the ratio of infrared to H30α flux being 52, all indicative of low metallicity star forming galaxies. We found the ratio of UV to H30α flux to be 3.5, and the ratio

We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be orbit equivalent if and only if they are conjugate, provided the group in question remains unchanged. However, this equivalency breaks down when considering other virtually cyclic groups like the direct product of the integer group and a non-abelian finite simple group, especially when these are used instead of the infinite dihedral group. Furthermore, this new result leads to the discovery of new orbit equivalence classes of continuous minimal actions on the closed surfaces carried by the direct product of the integer group and a non-abelian finite simple group.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ is not compact. We also establish that kernel-based techniques outperform traditional parametric methods like Galerkin methods in terms of convergence. Moreover, this research offers a new perspective on the limiting object of nonparametric estimates of $P$. Furthermore, it is shown that these findings are significant for various spectral analysis techniques for Markov transition operators. Our study also provides a novel, nontrivial application of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces in probability theory, in particular, for the study of linear stochastic differential equations driven by pure jump processes.

Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves upon previous designs by reducing estimation error and offers more accurate conditions for the convergence of estimation outcomes. To validate this innovation, the proposed method is applied to the SIR epidemic model, thereby addressing the state estimation requirements for both nonlinear and linear systems efficiently and contributing new knowledge to the field.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models. We propose an alternative point of view, where the boost offered by temporal models is limited. The key to achieving this may lie in the choice of comparison. We introduce a novel baseline approach, named TLink, that effectively linearly combines the predictions generated by a selection of static state-of-the-art models, demonstrating superior performance on fully observable temporal knowledge graphs. Additionally, TLink boasts the advantages of enhanced interpretability, reduced computational requirements, and ease of implementation. The efficacy of TLink is showcased through its performance in accurately predicting link connections in fully observable temporal knowledge graphs, as well as in fully observable and partially observable temporal knowledge graphs challenged by missing time frames. The evaluation of TLink includes a thorough examination of its performance across fully observable and partially observable temporal knowledge graphs.

Research driven by ultrashort pulses from Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators has spawned diverse applications, with theoretical understanding rooted in conventional beam propagation analysis. However, established frameworks are often insufficient for handling the extreme demands of high-power oscillators. This study expands upon the ABCD-matrix method to investigate ring resonators in high-power settings, also offering critical guidance for maintaining stable Kerr-lens mode-locking in high-power pulse applications.

Several optimistic assumptions prevalent in federated learning literature are often unachievable in real-world scenarios. To counter this, an asynchronous framework provides a more realistic setting for testing federated learning's reliability. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accounts for delayed client participation and periodic server refreshes. A novel regression model was developed to leverage the asynchronous setting and implement robust predictive techniques. This is the first successful implementation of robust predictive federated learning in an asynchronous environment. Due to the asynchronous nature, a conventional gradient descent update formula cannot be applied. To resolve this, an online filtering approach was proposed, evaluated at participating clients, and transmitted to the server. The model utilizes summary statistics to reduce communication load, enhancing efficiency. Experimental results using nonlinear datasets reveal superior performance compared to conventional federated learning models, particularly under resource-constrained settings.

To improve the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells with limited light absorption, researchers investigate a back reflector with a nanostructured 3D photonic band gap crystal made from silicon that can easily be integrated into the existing thin films.  A numerical approach is used to compute the optical properties of these new solar cell designs by solving for light and electrons simultaneously and calculating the absorbed power within the film.  The findings show that employing a 3D photonic band gap crystal back reflector can boost the absorption in films as thin as 2500 Angstroms by increasing the total absorbed light by a factor of 1.56.  This suggests that these new solar cell designs can operate effectively without needing thinner films, at a height of less than 2500 Angstroms.

We have derived a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$, which, when the absolute value of $s$ tends to infinity in the right half-plane, behave similarly to iterated exponentials. These functions are linked to nested exponentials through a useful functional equation and have a series expansion that converges within a certain region of the complex plane. By examining the properties of $\beta$, we can study the dynamics of the exponential map $e^{\mu z}$ and obtain insights into the behavior of fractional iterations. Our analysis allows us to identify conditions under which Abel equations can be constructed from $\beta$ and to identify holomorphic functions of period $2\pi i / \lambda$ that serve as Abel functions of the form $t(s+1) = e^{\mu t(s)}$.

We introduce a novel construction of high dimensional eigenvector-preserving projections, derived from the random covering of simplicial complexes. Our method encompasses various types of random coverings, resulting in diverse sets of dimensional projections, including ones analogous to Markov's double covering of the simplex and its consequences for Markov partitions. This allows us to obtain improved eigenvalue bounds for certain graphs, including Krasikov-Aldroul's construction, in addition to establishing the existence of dimensional projections for vast classes of spherical functions, an area of study originally presented by Markov.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments on GdInO3 and similar materials.

The application of graph embedding for predicting links in complex networks has shown remarkable success, but most real-world networks are sparse, which are currently underserved by this field. We propose the Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) model, which creates a representation of network nodes suitable for predicting links in these types of sparse networks. Initially, our model converts the network's adjacency matrix into a Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM) before passing it through a neural network for a dimensionally-reduced representation. Notably, our neural network-based approach can be considered an alternate method of performing singular value decomposition. Finally, our approach utilizes the generated feature matrix to compute node similarities, which are pivotal in predicting links. Through thorough experimentation using both synthetic and actual sparse networks, our research demonstrates the superiority of SSNE over existing methods, showcasing its effectiveness across various scenarios.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to achieve a deep silicon cell suitable for holding a flammable mixture of hydrogen and air, thereby enabling the development of a highly sensitive silicon pyroelectric sensor. This cell, about 1.8 mm deep, is capable of holding two vapor layers from separate chambers. The resulting device is highly effective as a pyroelectric sensor due to its novel geometry and deep silicon cells, exhibiting responsiveness in the infrared region and ability to detect extremely thin layers of vapor within a hydrogen-air mixture. Furthermore, the device is able to provide compensation for thermal noise due to its mass which helps in infrared vibration damping. The device performance is evaluated using hydrogen and methane gas mixtures and its potential application in life science research and environmental monitoring is also explored.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Preemptive wildfire monitoring is critical for forest safety and environmental protection.
Developing effective methods for inferring visible images from infrared images of wildfires is
essential for early detection and monitoring. We introduce FIRe-GAN, a deep learning framework that
uses a cycle-consistency trained U-net architecture to enhance low-quality visible images and produce
high-fidelity inferred images. Experimentation with the WM-COVID19 dataset shows that our approach surpasses
the performance of conventional image processing techniques and state-of-the-art deep learning methodologies.

Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe repercussions, making the utilization of multiple detection methods necessary, particularly when they do not rely on physical examinations. Observing social media expression patterns is highly advantageous for identifying mental health, since individuals tend to convey their emotions openly on these platforms. While depression is uncommon on mainstream social media due to users' desire for positive online images, recognizing subtle indications is vital to accurately diagnose the condition. Since limited research is conducted in depression detection, primarily due to the absence of suitable datasets and accurate classification models, we developed a data set derived from Facebook posts that exhibit various levels of depression symptom severity. The data set comprises 20,502 posts from 8,192 users, each categorized into one of four symptom severity levels: none, mild, moderate, or severe. To establish a benchmark for future studies, we employed traditional machine learning methods to analyze the data set and discovered that logistic regression successfully predicted severe depression symptoms in 35.3% of users, outperforming raw text prediction methods. Moreover, we discovered that individuals who employed more slang terms while exhibiting severe depression symptom severity, whereas those using fewer slang terms were associated with minor symptom severity.

We've developed two probabilistic models for the COVID-19 pandemic, incorporating the UK government's guidelines for social distancing to quantify the impact of these measures. Our primary model tracks the progression of the disease based on the number of close contacts an individual has, while a secondary model considers the number of close contacts more thoroughly. Both models estimate the probability of infection and the number of people affected at any given time. By comparing our forecasts to real data, we've demonstrated that our stochastic model based on the SIS format is accurate, generating minimal differences between predicted and actual values. A stochastic model incorporating the SIR format, however, shows more deviation from reality. In addition to examining the SIR and SIS scenarios, we're also examining other probabilistic models with modified epidemic patterns, all driven by the goal of providing the most precise pandemic forecasts to aid public policy decisions.

The ISGMR and a $K = 0$ component of the ISGQR in severely deformed nuclei exhibit a strong interrelation, manifesting as a distinctive double peak structure in the isoscalar monopole (IS0) strength distribution. A specific low-energy deformation-induced peak, alongside the dominant broad ISGMR part, is identified in the IS0 spectrum. Notably, the narrow low-lying ISGMR peak is distinctively linked to the rotational deformation in the ISGQR, known as the second collective excited state, possessing $K = 0$ symmetry. Computations using the density-displacement method, incorporating the influence of IS0 and IS2 strength, successfully reproduce the double-peaked IS0 spectrum observed in deformed nuclei. Furthermore, the reduced beta deformation parameter $\delta_2$ derived from the IS0 strength distribution through this method, is found to be in line with the value obtained from the IS2 strength distribution, thus highlighting the significance of the IS0-$\delta_2$ strength coupling in describing nuclear deformation.

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, is confirmed through analytical means. Theoretical findings reveal that the system can only converge asymptotically, involving multiple sequences of stick-slip cycles, regardless of the starting conditions. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical models through diverse examples of convergence.

A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities and derivatives using historical data only. Key aspects of this approach involve leveraging various derivative types such as forwards, futures, options, and taking into account factors such as trading costs, liquidity constraints and other frictions. This algorithm can effectively handle portfolios of any nature and features continuous action and state spaces with a risk-adjusted objective. Most notably, the model allows for the derivation of an actor-critic algorithm capable of improving investment strategies and reducing the risk of the portfolio without the need for model simulation, possible under the condition that the value function meets certain criteria. Support is also provided for the creation of a compatible Bellman target network and suggestions for the initial portfolio strategy and the learning rate scheduling are offered. Further research demonstrates the capacity of the model to efficiently handle synthetic derivatives hedging, account balance constraints and other practical investment issues.

In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term engagement. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred unobserved user intent from historical data. Our approach also allows for the dynamic discovery of user intent. In contrast to existing studies, which focus solely on the likelihood of user response to recommended items, our approach considers the interplay of user intent and item visibility when making inferences. We've developed a new probabilistic framework for sequential recommenders that integrates user intent modeling and item visibility. Our framework can also accommodate discoveries of hidden user intent. We've represented the recommended items and user intent as vectors, allowing for their natural combination to produce a visible recommendation in 3D space. Our approach allows for the traditional max-margin ranking loss and a novel loss function that takes into account the changing nature of user intent. Our results, derived from both synthetic and real data, demonstrate the effectiveness of our model and loss function, and our code is freely available for public use.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out due to its unique unfolding into a Fuchsian equation through a general symmetric solution. Notably, this particular equation is the first instance of a Fuchs equation known to admit a general symmetric solution. A key characteristic of the DCH equation is its Fuchsian nature in a two-parameter space when limits are taken: one parameter approaches infinity, and the other remains finite. A notable observation about the DCH equation's Fuchsian boundary is the emergence of a singular point at the origin, and a fundamental question arises as to whether the DCH equation is a unique manifestation of a Fuchsian nature within a three-parameter space. Our study seeks to address this query by combining the DCH equation with a Fuchsian nature in a three-parameter space consisting of a three-dimensional Euclidean space equipped with a Birkhoff invariant, and a monodromy defomation that transcends the identity.

Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation in an infinite-dimensional setting where a fixed number of matrix components is considered. These findings are based on an innovative model transformation from the homogeneous to a heterogeneous low-rank matrix tensor product model. We demonstrate that some PCA-based methods are optimal in many situations but we also identify scenarios where they fall short and an alternative covariance recovery approach is proposed to overcome these shortfalls. Furthermore, by extending these results to a finite sample setting, we establish performance benchmarks for various PCA-based and maximum likelihood methods that can be inherited by their Bayesian counterparts.

In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is uncovered, where an extra exceptional point in the bulk material is safeguarded by its connection to boundary states.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. This combined observable enhances our capacity to detect potential violations of short distance origin Lepton Flavour Universality, all while retaining a straightforward theoretical explanation if a deviation from its predicted value, close to one, is observed.

This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations.

We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on randomly sampled CT volumes, and subsequent steps utilize the network to extract embedding features from the full scan volume. Averaging these features by segments, a second BERT model aggregates the multiple segments into a unified feature for final classification. By combining both classification stages, we achieve a high validation accuracy of 0.9164 in macro F1 score.

Network science is the multidisciplinary study of intricate systems, which can be represented as interconnected networks consisting of nodes and edges with various attributes. These seemingly straightforward structures conceal an extraordinary depth of complexity due to their capability to encapsulate a wide array of real-world phenomena, encompassing chemical reactions, biological pathways, social connections, and other intricate relationships. Mastering network science necessitates the mastery of a comprehensive toolkit spanning numerous fields of study, including graph and probability theory, linear algebra, machine learning, combinatorics, and statistical physics.

This comprehensive resource is designed to provide foundational knowledge of these diverse analytical tools. It aims to equip readers with an all-encompassing understanding of these approaches, allowing them to develop their expertise as specialists in network science. This book serves as an invaluable roadmap for aspiring network scientists, guiding them through the rich tapestry of this rapidly evolving field. Network science is distinguished by its interdisciplinary roots, having emerged from diverse fields such as mathematics, computer science, and sociology. This book seeks to forge a new path forward, one that defines the field as an independent and distinctive area of study with its unique applications and research perspectives.

Network science is uniquely positioned to provide insights into some of the most pressing issues of our time, including recommendations for content sharing, route optimization in transportation and logistics, drug interaction mapping, climate modeling, and social segmentation. As an independent field of study, network science is poised to leave a lasting impact on our lives and the world around us, from the

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as evidenced by the rapid changes observed in Trinidadian guppies and other laboratory models. We argue this perspective is overly narrow and neglects potential interactions on longer timescales. Ecology and evolution can, and do, change at different rates. For a full understanding of eco-evolutionary dynamics, we need to incorporate insights from multiple timescales, spanning millions of years. Modulators such as population size, climate change, and genetic variation influence evolution and interaction rates between these processes. To broaden the scope of eco-evolutionary research, we need to combine theories from paleontology, evolutionary biology, and ecology to develop a more comprehensive and unified theory.

A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations by comparing various speech models with minimal adjustments to improve downstream performance. By showing that self-supervised speech models can excel in multiple downstream tasks with little adaptation, SUPERB highlights a significant paradigm in the speech field that needs to be studied more. Specifically, assessing the ability of speech models to resist malicious attacks under the control of knowledgeable and inexperienced adversaries has become a high priority in the speech community. In this research, we make a first effort to test the potential vulnerability of speech models to both types of adversaries through experiments that generate effective countermeasures. The experiments show that speech models developed in the SUPERB paradigm are particularly susceptible to attacks launched by adversaries lacking extensive knowledge, and the crafted attacks by expert adversaries exhibit portability across various scenarios. Moreover, our XAB testing process confirms the undetectability of generated attacks by adversaries.

Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for market liquidity suppliers under circumstances of heightened token price volatility. 
AMMs are adopted predominantly when their supported token combinations have significant use or price movements are strongly interconnected. 
However, the steeper pricing curve actually diminishes arbitrage challenges, though this benefits investors at a decreased rate. 
Conversely, the inclusion of numerous tokens worsens the arbitrage dilemma. 
We furnish empirical support for our primary model outcomes by using detailed transaction records of AMMs.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. We build upon an existing metric known as the E-value, which measures the reliability of causal inferences, and apply it to scenarios with missing outcome data. Through case studies on Facebook's partially-observed conversion events, we develop an approach to conduct large-scale sensitivity analysis by contributing three key improvements. First, we develop a Bayesian estimation technique for sensitivity parameters using unreliable benchmarks that respect data privacy; both objective and subjective initial probability distributions are explored. Second, we leverage the Bayesian estimation of sensitivity parameters to introduce a simulation-based approach for inferring the E-value's posterior distribution. Lastly, we derive closed-form distributions for the E-value that enable direct inference in scenarios where posterior simulation is infeasible due to computational limitations. We showcase improved performance over the existing asymptotic inference method using data-driven simulations and complement this with an actual analysis of Facebook's conversion events.

This study concludes a comprehensive categorization of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the larger framework of the extended quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q\big[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}\big]$. Firstly, prior research by the author concerning symmetries involving the Cartan generator(s) with non-trivial actions, and those exhibiting generic behavior, are revisited and verified. A thorough enumeration of non-generic symmetries then follows. These combined categories collectively form an exhaustive compilation of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries in the context of $\mathbb{C}_q\big[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}\big]$.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding sensitive data and addressing concerns about privacy within IoVs. Another developing technology, Blockchain, has the potential to significantly reduce costs and improve block verification rates in FL settings. This study conducts an extensive analysis of current BL-FL research, identifying common challenges and limitations, and highlighting essential components that must be considered in future research. Specifically, this literature review examines the current state of BL-FL architecture, evaluates FL frameworks, and analyzes security features and functional components of BL-FL systems. It also delves into the existing challenges and future research directions in BL-FL frameworks for IoVs, with a focus on using FL for secure IoVs data collection and FL-based traffic management systems.

The ALICE experiment has recorded the $p_\mathrm{T}$ distribution of D meson production, including both prompt and non-prompt (formed in beauty-hadron decays), in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV, and focused on data with an integrated luminosity of approximately 19.3 nb^-1. D mesons were identified through their decays into different hadronic combinations, such as $\mathrm{D^0 \to #kappa#kappa}$ and $\mathrm{D_s^+\to \varphi \pi^+\to \mathrm{K}^{*0} \mathrm{K}^{+}}$. Non-prompt D meson production was found to have a different $p_\mathrm{T}$ distribution than prompt D mesons, and this was used to disentangle the two signal components. The production cross-section of D mesons from beauty-hadron decays was found to be higher than expected and showed the highest yield for the lowest $p_\mathrm{T}$ range when compared to data at different centre-of-mass energies. The ratio of charm to beauty hadron production was also measured but found to be consistent across different $p_\mathrm{T}$ with a corresponding value of around 0.57 when compared to bottom quark production.

The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures using a novel cryogenic platform. 
This infrastructure will be built into a fully functional experimental setting within a controlled magnetic environment within the clean room of a 42-Kelvin cryogenic shield, encompassing cutting-edge millikelvin technology, superconducting magnets, and cryogen-free design. This document outlines the process of creating the platform, beginning with conceptual design and culminating in the completion of the experimental platform.

Previous research indicates a high prevalence of misused crypto APIs in Java and C, but similar studies for other languages have been absent, with one notable exception - a study conducted on professional developers in Python revealed a relatively lower incidence of insecure code for crypto-related tasks. This paper seeks to investigate the prevalence of insecure crypto API usage in real-world Python projects hosted on GitHub by analyzing commit flows. Following established protocols, we first developed and disseminated ten cryptographic tasks to developers, collecting and comparing secure and insecure code submissions from them. This led to a characterization of the existing code submissions that utilize two widely-used crypto libraries in Python, pyCrypto and cryptography. Our analysis of 525 code submissions suggests a lower fraction of insecure submissions for pyCrypto (10G/28G), but a higher fraction for cryptography (1G/28G). Additionally, pyCrypto's low fraction of insecure submissions suggests that previous mitigation efforts in Python are effective. Our study also reveals several security risks and unwelcome security features introduced by the insecure code submissions. Ultimately, our findings stress the significance of practical security research in programming languages and crypto, ultimately aiming to enhance the security of real-world Python code.

This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding superior results to current object positioning methods. A pivotal element of our framework is the object labelling process, where multiple, potentially inaccurate two-dimensional annotations are compiled and merged to produce an accurate result. To achieve this, our method relies on diverse image datasets, acquired through differing search parameters, captured by different individuals, and filtered by specific criteria. Furthermore, to optimize performance, we have developed an algorithm that dynamically adjusts the size of these datasets in accordance with the objects' spatial dimensions, prioritizing coverage of smaller objects within the environment. By combining these strategies, our framework enables the achievement of high object detection precision across large-scale, dense metropolitan environments. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our method at reducing the average distance between detected and actual object locations, yielding improvements of 44.8% and 26.9% for smaller and larger objects, respectively, when compared to a leading object positioning method.

We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method involving both convex and non-convex regularization terms to yield l0 pseudo-norm approximations. This leads to an iterative algorithm utilizing proximal averaging that can be reformatted as a trainable neural network, optimizing through data-driven training. Our effectiveness is proven through numerical evaluations using synthetic data from 1-D seismic traces and 2-D wedge models in comparison to established techniques. Furthermore, we provide additional validation with a simulated Marmousi2 model and real-world 3D seismic data from the Penobscot survey in Nova Scotia.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the coefficients that form power series. We establish that these conditions apply to both linear and nonlinear operators, particularly for those associated with elliptic equations and their counterparts in harmonic analysis.

Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion, which describe operator fusion. Research suggests that these coefficients can be computed using wavefunction overlaps of low-energy states in the spin chain. We have demonstrated that central charge, conformal dimensions, and operator product expansion coefficients are encoded in wavefunction overlaps, accompanied by universal corrections that rely on the model's infrared behavior. This approach allows for numerical determination of all the required quantities without relying on the exact solution of the model, and it was successfully applied to a Haagerup spin chain with various fillings. The exact wavefunctions of this model enabled us to compute the operator product expansion coefficients and central charge with high precision, confirming that the model has a non-degenerate ground state and conformal behavior in the critical point.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single tags with uncertainty, POS tagging algorithms should allow for probabilistic outcomes. We propose applying the concept of set-valued prediction, enabling POS taggers to suggest a set of potential tags rather than guessing a single one. The objective is to strike a balance between ensuring a high likelihood of the correct tag being included while minimizing the number of suggested candidates. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating set-valued prediction into existing state-of-the-art POS tagging algorithms yields more accurate and resilient results, particularly when encountering words not present in training datasets.

This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function. Using this method, we derive two new criteria that a demand function candidate must meet. First, it must be symmetrical and have a negatively semi-definite Slutsky matrix, and second, it must be a unique concave solution to a specific partial differential equation globally. Additionally, we establish under certain conditions that a demand function candidate that meets certain symmetry and negative semi-definiteness requirements will satisfy the first criterion. We also explore an application of these findings in a new approach to a general theorem for locally Lipschitz utilities.

As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, computer-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities stemming from language uncertainties. We have created an AI-powered system to automatically transform city needs into a formal expression, utilizing the KRL language, by leveraging semantic data and user feedback. The proposed approach is showcased through a real-world application involving city services for smart parking and rubbish collection. As part of the city management system, these services receive and process requests through a web interface, reinforcing the importance of formalization and highlighting the need for future research in this area.

Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of the quantum circuit is enhanced. This approach's effectiveness in real-world superconducting quantum devices is evaluated through simulations of the molecular binding energy for the hydrogen molecule. Our findings indicate that our method can effectively mitigate noise in these systems, leading to significant improvements in algorithm performance. Notably, our research also sheds light on the relationship between the length of the hidden inverse sequence – known as the hidden order – and the accuracy of the computed results. By optimizing the hidden order, the accuracy of the quantum algorithm can be substantially improved, leading to a significant improvement in binding energy computation with an increased hidden order.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective epimorphism may not yield a partial order. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by forming the cofibered image of the original preorder above the epimorphism. In categories satisfying regularity conditions, the existence of such a cofibered image of a partial order corresponds to the existence of the least upper bound among all partial orders within the category. This work explores general conditions ensuring the existence of these cofibered images, which can be used in the study of categorical logic and modal complexity.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and weather forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to standardize extreme outcomes. Results show a significant increase in the most severe weather occurrences over the past few decades, with largest outcomes at higher latitudes. A significant connection is found between wind and wave data, with largest outcomes linked to severe storms. Comparing satellite wind and wave data with forecasted data shows that the 2007-2018 satellite data exceeds the 1985-2010 forecast data in terms of extreme weather occurrences.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between datasets. To optimize visual-textual alignment for CLIP models on various tasks, we introduce a technique that refines image-text cross-modality learning via VT-CLIP. This process involves utilizing attention-driven mechanisms to direct text features toward informative visual regions, effectively enhancing visual-textual correlation for improved category-based matching. Subsequently, we demonstrate VT-CLIP's efficacy in few-shot classification scenarios on 11 prominent datasets.

To enhance the accuracy of computational models plagued by noisy data and parameters, this study address the issue of reducing error in linear systems with uncertain components. We investigate the phenomenon where slight changes to the system's parameters lead to substantial and uniformly directed reductions in the error margin. This concept is referred to as operator shifting. We develop a set of self-consistency conditions that can evaluate and quantify error reductions. In the context of matrix systems, we establish relationships between the degree of error reduction, matrix size, and residual norms. These relationships enable the calculation of the optimal shifting factor for achieving the greatest possible error reduction.
