The calculations were based on the use of virtual photons with both transverse and longitudinal momenta, which has been shown to affect the twist-6 precision calculations. The results show that the twist-6 contributions from the photon's virtualness are most noticeable at large values of the Bjorken variable x, which isn't the case at smaller values of x.

All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, characterized by their unpredictability and distinctness from human errors. A critical objective is to rectify these AI errors without compromising their established abilities and ideally without requiring direct human intervention. This report outlines an innovative approach aimed at boosting the cognitive capabilities of individual AI systems by collaborating with other AIs. It synthesizes insights from multi-agent learning systems and introduces novel mathematical techniques for non-recursive corrections of legacy AI errors. This study develops a foundational framework for non-destructive AI corrections and derives a sequence of probabilistic separation theorems, serving as a powerful tool for evaluating machine learning algorithms and their capacity to rectify their own errors without human involvement. Furthermore, our approach facilitates an in-depth analysis of various numerical solving methods for non-linear programs, providing a novel criterion for assessing a solver's ability to identify and rectify its own mistakes.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling originating from a mean-field state. By introducing a fully superfluid state with a vortical order that is intrinsically linked to the spin-orbit coupling, we observe two distinct thermal phase transitions: one related to the disappearance of the vortical order and the other characterised by the loss of superfluidity. Through a combination of numerical calculations at zero momentum and theoretical developments, we have determined the critical temperatures for these transitions and demonstrated that they follow standard critical power laws. Furthermore, we have validated the validity of our theoretical approach by comparing it with quantum Monte Carlo simulations and observed strong agreement between the two methods.

Consider two groups, G_1 and G_2, and suppose a homomorphism \phi from G_1 to G_2 maps a particular element to another element. In the context of graph theory, this leads to the concept of a group G_1 degraphizing another group G_2, which translates to graphs G_1 and G_2 representing the same design. Up to a certain point, research focused on identifying all possible groups that degraphize one another. Every finite abelian group was examined in a previous study, which found some groups degraphize others, and others do not. Building on this previous research, this work continues to investigate the relationships between finite abelian groups, determine which do not degraphize one another, and identifies the underlying reasons for these cases.

Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional settings, are explored, taking into account both static and dynamic frameworks. We concentrate on type IIA string theory with interwoven $U(1)$-gauged $SP(2)$ and $SO(3)$ symmetries, incorporating charged superfields that contribute to the theory's enhanced global structure. The corresponding dual geometries comprise AdS$_2$ and AdS$_3$ spacetimes, replete with charged, non-trivial, and non-Ricci flat geometry. These findings encompass both supersymmetric and non-supersymmetric solutions, encompassing a novel sector of the system characterized by a non-Abelian $SO(3)$ global symmetry. Furthermore, type IIA solutions with charged superpartners are presented to illustrate the significant potential of the scheme. Moreover, a dynamic framework is developed, building upon a modified version of the Hubeny-Marolf-Sanchez-Strassler (HMSS) prescription for low-dimensional anti-de Sitter solutions, which exhibit partial translation invariance due to dynamic $SP(2)$ symmetry and, consequently, yield an accurate account of the dual conformal data.

In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a pivotal step. Gaussian Processes excel in regression and classification tasks, largely due to their ability to leverage kernel functions that mimic various types of data relationships. Traditionally, these kernel functions are devised by experts using their in-depth knowledge of the problem at hand or through a time-consuming process of trial and error. This research proposes a novel, data-driven method for gauging the suitability of kernel functions by analytically examining their impact on Gaussian Process regression predictions in terms of variance and mean. Combining this analysis with a genetic algorithm allows us to generate, from a set of fundamental mathematical expressions, kernel functions that closely replicate the performances of established kernels on test data, as evidenced by our findings on time series and calibration data.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to in-flight decays of
muons from the beam line, which produce in-flight decay background beams. This
background leads to a significant beam-induced background bias in collider
measurements. A potential solution is to reduce background by widening the
detector acceptance at the cost of decreased luminosity. In this paper, we
investigate methods to improve detector design and optimize analysis strategies
to minimize the impact of in-flight decay background on collider measurements.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and gradually shifts towards optimizing the parameters with a focus on promoting inter-parameter interactions. Spartan offers flexibility by accommodating different regularization strengths and flexible parameter subsets, allowing it to be easily adapted and generalized. Spartan's effectiveness is showcased through successful application in achieving previously challenging sparsity levels on CNVP models for ImageNet-1M and VGG16 for CIFAR-10.

The intricate connection between many-particle interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in various thermal properties of materials and substances. To explore this relationship, our experiment featuring a cold atom technology focused on a one-dimensional weakly interacting Bose gas, where the effective spatial dimension was manipulated by modulating an external potential. Through an in-depth analysis of the experiment's results, our data revealed a significant, yet subtle, effect of Pauli blocking that deviates from both a mathematical model for a system with two spatial dimensions and a different theoretical approach. Furthermore, our experiment demonstrated that the temperature-dependent correlation length of the 1D Bose gas is influenced by both the kinetic energy associated with the system's transverse direction and the strength of the interparticle interactions.

Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation choices referred to as test smells. These shortcomings can significantly undermine the quality of software systems by exacerbating difficulties in comprehension, amplifying maintenance complexities, and making systems more susceptible to bugs and errors. Prior studies have investigated the likely consequences of test smells on test code. Despite their focus, a knowledge gap remains regarding the perspectives of developers regarding these issues. To fill this knowledge gap, a study empirically examined how software developers perceive the level of impact test smells have on test code. The research analyzed the perspectives of developers from six open-source projects, inquiring about the influence test smells have on test code and whether they consider it a pressing concern. The results indicate that while developers often view test smells as minor concerns for their own code, they recognize the potential for negative implications, particularly in terms of maintaining and evolving the project. The developers further emphasized that actively detecting and removing test smells from test code can have positive effects on the project overall.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the prox-regular moving set and two types of perturbations: a Carathéodory mapping and an integral forcing term with an integrand dependent on time variables. To address this new integro-differential sweeping process, a semi-discretization method is developed and used in conjunction with an original Gronwall-like inequality to prove that it possesses a single, absolutely continuous solution. Furthermore, the solution is demonstrated to be continuous with respect to its initial value. The obtained results have been successfully applied to two significant problems: nonlinear integro-differential complementarity systems, comprising Volterra equations and complementarity constraints, and non-standard electrical circuits with time-varying capacitors and diodes, representing novel aspects of the presented work.

We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating lepton and quark pair production through high-energy electron-positron annihilations. As the most advanced generator for this process, the code, now rewritten entirely in modern C++, maintains all features of its Fortran 77 predecessor, while incorporating several enhanced Monte Carlo algorithm improvements. Its capabilities, supplemented with next-to-leading order QED corrections, genuine weak corrections using the {\tt DIZET} library, and polarized $\tau$ decays facilitated by {\tt TAUOLA}, serve as a starting point for future updates to achieve the high precision needed for next-generation lepton colliders. Moreover, this version integrates {\tt HEPMC3}, a new interface that replaces {\tt HepEvt}, to connect the {\tt KKMCee} with other essential components such as parton showers and detector simulations. Specifically, this new interface enables the utilization of {\tt PHOTOS} for additional photon emissions in $\tau$ decays, now rewritten in the C++ language.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, leading research methods, such as the Ma et al. model, are not capable of handling signals with noise levels higher than 10 Hilbert transform units without degrading the inter-beat interval accuracy. A recently developed Tiramisu model has exhibited state-of-the-art performance in ECG-based identification tasks, and our study leverages its potential to improve inter-beat interval estimation while addressing the limitation of only handling signals with moderate noise levels. We achieved this by combining the Tiramisu model with pre-processed raw ECG signals, which, when compared to the reference method, demonstrated a 67% reduction in inter-beat interval estimation error at signal noise levels of 20 Hilbert transform units and a 25% improvement in signal with zero noise conditions.

To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing the communication cost associated with data transfer, especially when calculating the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in just a few data passes. The prevailing subspace randomized methods used to compute the t-SVD require either 2q + 2 or q + 1 data passes depending on the implementation for any positive integer q. Our proposed randomized algorithm for t-SVD is compatible with a contemporary subspace randomized approach but reduces the necessary data passes to q, making it a more efficient solution. The new algorithm also provides an innovative way to compute the k-dimensional tensor segmentation matrix, which is a crucial element in the t-SVD calculation. Furthermore, we have adapted our algorithm for computing the k-largest tensor singular values and their corresponding decomposed factors using only q data passes.

Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and visualization, but this approach struggles to accommodate dynamic behavior exhibited by real-world networks. To offer a comprehensive overview of embedding dynamic graphs, this work defines key properties and categorizes embedding techniques. It showcases the efficacy of embedding static graphs in dynamic settings, before highlighting the advantages of purpose-designed methods that incorporate temporal dynamics. Notably, a substantial portion of research in this area focuses on improving embedding algorithms for static graphs. However, we find that these approaches often overlook crucial aspects like edge direction and node persistence when static graph embedding is applied to temporal networks. To counter this limitation, we present representative techniques that tackle edge direction and node permanence in temporal networks. Finally, we outline areas for future research, highlighting potential avenues for advancement.

To investigate the 3He + 4n system, specifically focusing on 7H's ground state, various models including the fuzzy light nucleus approach, Faddeev equations, and the cusp method are being used. This investigation aims to determine if 7H's ground state can be accurately described as a 3He + 4n resonance. To begin, a theoretical analysis using the fuzzy light nucleus approach will be employed, followed by a more rigorous examination with the Faddeev equations, with both assessments supported by recent experimental data. This study will provide a comprehensive understanding of the 3He + 4n system and will determine if 7H's ground state can be classified as a resonance.

This research paper investigates a Nirenberg type problem on the upper half spheres with the aim of finding conformal metrics that satisfy a prescribed scalar curvature and zero mean curvature on the boundary. The investigation is focused on solving a boundary value problem, denoted as (P), that incorporates the critical Sobolev exponent. The equation (P) involves a nonlinear term with the exponent (n+2)/(n-2) and can be stated as:

$(P)$

$\begin{cases}
   \nabla^2 u -  \frac{n(n-2)}{4}u = Ku^{ \frac{n+2}{n-2}},\ u>0
  in  S^n_+,\\ 
 \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu}= 0
 on $\partial  S^n_+$.

\end{cases}$ 

A function K, with $K\in C^2(S^n_+)$ and K > 0, appears in the equation. The existence of finite energy solutions is shown for a subcritical approximation of (P) under certain generic conditions on the function K, resulting in solutions with multiple clusters of zeros on the boundary. Utilizing the Stoynyak region, it is demonstrated that solutions with multiple clusters up to $n-3$ can be constructed. The solutions are then shown to be smooth via a removal of singularities procedure, a method initially developed by Murthy and Nirenberg. As an additional

Deep Metric Learning methods primarily aim to develop a space where data similarities can be accurately maintained. These methods have made notable improvements in many tasks such as classification, clustering, and retrieval, with the added benefit of being able to directly optimize similarity measures over embedding space. However, the widely accepted loss functions used in many metrics have several drawbacks such as not having a well-defined gradient w.r.t. metric parameters and being susceptible to noisy gradients. This noise can often result in unstable optimization performance. To address these limitations, the loss functions used have been modified in a proxy metric setting, where gradients are defined analytically. However, the proxy metric approach has not yet perfectly optimized the desired metric, as confirmed by recent theoretical studies. In an effort to overcome this limitation, the presented work uses the Sinkhorn divergence, a theoretically well-established metric, to develop a loss function that can be directly optimized and is sensitive to the underlying data structure. This is, however, complicated by the non-differentiable nature of the Sinkhorn divergence, where a proxy metric-based gradient is employed to facilitate stochastic gradient descent optimization. The results of the experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in a large-scale person re-identification task.

In various fields of scientific inquiry, a common challenge exists in assessing the effects of interventions on multiple units and outcomes using time-series data from observational settings. To address this issue, we've devised a novel method combining established approaches based on a factor analysis model with difference-in-differences analysis. This novel method is then applied to an analysis of the COVID-19 contact tracing system in England to assess the impact of local tracing partnerships on the system's performance. Our results indicate a substantial increase in the system's performance after partnerships were established, with the largest improvements observed in London.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey provides precise stellar data for many clusters, including Melotte 72. With a total of 1,035 stars, including 41 blue stars, three Cepheids, and 14 probable cluster members among the red stars, I derived the cluster's fundamental parameters by implementing several methods on magnitudes in different bands. The resulting photometric transformations yield a distance of $8.38^{+0.39}_{-0.38}$ kpc, $8.62^{+0.42}_{-0.41}$ kpc, and $8.04^{+0.39}_{-0.38}$ kpc in Gaia DR1 blue, GALEX FUV, and GALEX NUV respects respectively, as well as a mass of $15,600-21,300 \times (d/8.5)^2$. Moreover, the contents analysis of the cluster reveal 0.35 \pm 0.15 brown dwarfs and 0.36 \pm 0.15 red dwarfs per square parsec, while the Cepheids' mean pulsation period is estimated to be six days. Additionally, the double star nature of the magnetic field regulator, HD 208540, as the cluster's prime magnetic field source, is further established.

Data analysis applications in medicine, cosmology, and materials science are witnessing growing interest in probabilistic excursion patterns. This research provides the first thorough examination of Betti numbers under a related probabilistic model involving Gaussian fields with shifting components, where the shift points follow a Poisson distribution. This work determines the asymptotic values of typical Betti numbers as the dimension of the Gaussian field grows while the density remains constant, specifically for a dimension determined by the correlation length as the correlation function varies. A related algorithm is used to precisely calculate certain excursion patterns associated with homology events, where the results are then applied to a related probabilistic model involving random walks, where a threshold is applied to the walk path, where the results are then used to find the expected values of homology events, which in turn are used to find certain expected excursion patterns associated with a related model involving percolation on a two-dimensional lattice.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using an image is a significant task that has been studied extensively. Yet, existing methods require a sequence of real-world images, which limits their applications in scenarios where robots operate autonomously. To address this issue, we propose a novel, image-based calibration technique that uses deep learning to relate camera images to intrinsic parameters. By utilizing large-scale simulated data with varying conditions, our approach simulates real-world scenarios like lighting changes and obstacles. The proposed method demonstrates an accurate prediction of intrinsic parameters with minimal actual experimental data required for validation. Furthermore, we showcase the efficacy of this technique in practical applications, such as navigating rooms and avoiding obstacles.

In real-world settings, RL systems face challenges due to various constraints that are difficult to formalize mathematically. For RL applications, it is crucial to operate within predetermined limits to ensure safety and comply with regulations. This study introduces a novel approach – inverse constrained reinforcement learning (ICRL) – that enables RL systems to learn from expert data under a set of predefined constraints. These constraints can originate from various sources, such as cost functions or benchmark observations. The proposed ICRL approach adapts an RL policy to comply with these constraints by optimizing it in conjunction with a constraint-predicting model. We demonstrate that ICRL can be resolved using a constrained optimization problem with a guaranteed global solution. Our experiments confirm the efficacy of ICRL on challenging navigation tasks with diverse constraint types like goal-based, safety, and feature-based constraints.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of the galaxy by studying a small percentage of the 100 billion stars within it, with the ultimate goal of producing a map to an unparalleled degree of accuracy. This article will examine the mission itself, along with the resulting data releases and their potential impact. A detailed overview of the DR1 and DR2 data releases and their initial findings, including DR1 as a precursor to the eagerly anticipated DR2, will also be presented.

For graphs with a given number of vertices and a specific value of their treewidth, we have created an algorithm that finds a specific type of sub-divided tree under the condition that it does not exceed a certain size. This new tree contains all the critical vertices of the original graph and can be generated efficiently in terms of storage needs. Additionally, we have devised another algorithm that finds a specific type of sub-divided tree within the same parameters. This new tree contains all the critical vertices of the original graph and can be generated efficiently in terms of storage needs. Furthermore, we have established a relationship between the sizes of these two trees and proved it through a rigorous mathematical argument. Finally, we have applied these two algorithms to develop efficient algorithms for computing other important characteristics of graphs, such as vertex and clique cover. These new algorithms achieve a significant reduction in storage needs compared to existing methods.

A substantial portion of network information is lost when converting directed graphs to undirected or symmetric versions, particularly when edge directions hold significant importance. To effectively capture local structure, researchers have developed and applied various measures such as degree-based and weighted versions of the C-statistic. Although previous discussions on these measures often focus on their general applications, they rarely consider their specific shortcomings and the specific limitations and requirements they impose. This study examines the underlying principles of weighted C-statistic and its symmetric counterpart to clarify their usage, constraints, and expectations in practical network analysis. It also differentiates between micro- and macro-level applications of these measures, highlighting that the former involves detecting local patterns while the latter involves identifying general trends. This work specifically looks at their performance in directed graphs, particularly when dealing with multiple edge types, inferred networks, and the analysis of measured networks, which often fall under the micro-category. To address these issues, the study proposes C*statistic as an alternative for undirected weighted graphs and develops a combination of this measure with a degree-based metric called the wC* statistic for directed weighted graphs, demonstrating their effectiveness in specific scenarios.

One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper focuses on the practical implementation of PINNs for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs). It outlines a precise methodology for determining the approximate errors of PINNs and evaluates its practical utility. The method can be used to assess the reliability of PINNs deployed in real-world applications and provides a systematic approach for improving the design of PINNs.

For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. Leveraging advances in big data analytics and machine learning has led to breakthroughs in air pollution modeling frameworks. This discussion highlights recent breakthroughs and proposes enhancements from the viewpoints of geostatistics and machine learning. Future developments will integrate learning algorithms with spatial analysis, allowing for the incorporation of spatial correlations in the modeling process. This integration is expected to improve the precision of existing air pollution models, thereby enhancing exposure assessments.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this design leads to broader peaks, and their shift towards lower bias voltages can be described using Drude theory. Given that Majorana peaks remain relatively unchanged by temperature, our findings provide a new criterion to identify topological superconductors: if the peak's shape and position exhibits little change with increasing temperature, it is more likely that the origin of the peak is from a Majorana mode.

We have established a non-asymptotic lower bound for the eigenvalues of a design matrix, generated by linear bandit algorithms that incur sub-linear regret in action spaces with constant curvature. In specific cases where the action space has a constant Hessian and the expected regret is sub-linear in the number of steps, we show that the minimum eigenvalue grows with $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for large $n$. In contrast to previously observed logarithmic growth, these "locally rich" action spaces force polynomial growth, effectively shifting the analysis towards a polynomial rather than a logarithmic lower bound. Notably, unlike the previous result, which was proven asymptotically as $n \to \infty$, this result holds at any point in time. Moreover, under a mild technical assumption, we obtain a lower bound with high probability. To further demonstrate the practical implications of our finding, we show that our spectral bound is particularly useful for tackling real-world challenges, such as model selection and clustering, in the context of linear bandits. In model selection, we leverage our spectral bound to prove that certain epoch-based algorithms adapt to the complexity of the model at an exponential rate, whereas for clustering, we show that by taking the spectral bounds into consideration, agents can infer the number of the cluster's components without needing to know this number beforehand.

Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows, determined by specific indices, are observed.  However, we find that this effect can be explained by another phenomenon, the orbital Hall effect, where the indices used to predict the behavior can be replaced by a more fundamental property, the orbital momentum.  Using the established orbital quantum mechanics methods, we are able to calculate the orbital Hall conductivity and show that it mirrors the behavior of valley Hall conductivity.  Furthermore, we are able to offer a new, alternative explanation for observed phenomena in this field.

The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models and crowd-sourced attacks on data. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches that use direct gradient optimization. This work aims to explore the novel threat of data manipulation during training (Data Poisoning) targeting Graph Classification neural networks via Reinforcement Learning agents. To this end, two scenarios of data poisoning are developed and two Graph Convolutional Neural Network benchmarks are selected for testing. Additionally, methods for detecting poisoning are introduced, including the integration of a robust agent within the learning process to counter poisoning and promote classification accuracy.

The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects from different sources are not aligned. To overcome this challenge, the standard astrometric cat-alogue matching process was augmented with a novel photometric alignment technique. This new method was combined with an existing time-weighted astrometric algorithm and demonstrated improved accuracy when operated in tandem. To support the development of this new photometric alignment algorithm, two new functionalities were incorporated into the MicCat cat-alogue matcher: the ability to perform single-object astrometric and photometric alignment, as well as to realign objects that have been previously matched to ensure the accuracy of the source association throughout the process. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed micCat matcher, the method was tested on two sets of photometric catalogs, one generated through simulations and the other sourced from actual multi-band image sets of a specific region, allowing for the validation against a known ground truth. The findings showed that the incorporation of the photometric information led to a reduction of 0.03 arcseconds in the average offset, while the matched source number increased by 1.7% when using MicCat with the astrometric and photometric astrometric alignment methods in comparison to using astrometric alone. Additionally, the proposed MicCat matcher was found to be adaptable for real-time source association as objects are processed through a real-time pipeline, revealing that MicCat is capable of providing a reliable source association even at the beginning of the pipeline,

In this paper, a hypergraph is considered as the family of its edges, and a hypergraph is said to possess property C if every edge has a minimum number of vertices greater than or equal to k, and we investigate the highest ratio of the largest to the smallest size of k-miminal vertex covers in a series of structures, and we prove that for an infinite hypergraph with property C and a given k, the size of its k-minimal vertex covers varies continuously and therefore the size of k-miminal vertex covers in an infinite hypergraph is determined uniquely, and we further determine the size of k-miminal vertex covers in particular types of structures, and we also investigate the size of EXS, the hypergraph in which every subset of an edge has a size different by at most one compared to the edge's size, and we establish that EXS has a size equal to k(m+n+1) for any k, and we further determine the size of EXS for particular types of structures, and n EXS contains an (n+1)-uniform subhypergraph for any n.

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates an icicle plot and a cooccur plot in a coordinated view, allowing users to identify and distinguish between hierarchical and non-hierarchical associations. OntoPlot's capabilities are further enhanced by integrated exploration tools, a focus area zooming mechanism, and a novel association browsing system, facilitating in-depth understanding and context-aware navigation. By facilitating association discovery and learning through explanation, OntoPlot supports users in uncovering new knowledge within the ontology.

We introduce an innovative technique incorporating semi-supervised learning and inter-domain loss to enhance end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss is trained using a CycleGAN-based cycle-consistency approach, and we investigate its effectiveness across three language pairs, three waveform-to-text tasks, and two benchmark datasets. Our experiments reveal that the inter-domain loss contributes significantly to the end-to-end model's performance improvement. Moreover, we find that leveraging cycleGAN-based mapping to incorporate auxiliary objectives results in better generalization and more robust model performance, especially in tasks with limited training data.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to consistently achieve its predicted ideals. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments, particularly in navigating through multiple possible paths, where the initial prediction errors are high and varied. Therefore, we have developed a novel variant of the active inference approach. This variant intelligently selects environmental interactions, creating a new module that collaborates with the traditional mental framework. We have tested our method in a real-world self-navigating scenario where a robot needs to reach multiple destinations on a map. Our results show that the proposed approach not only creates a more accurate mental framework but also significantly reduces interactions by focusing on the most relevant paths.

Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations in the NVT ensemble to investigate the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we discovered a sharp change in the thermal diffusion coefficient. This shift was tied to the changes in composition and density of the mixture rather than the temperature. Furthermore, the penetration depth of the molecules varied with temperature, affecting their thermal diffusion. An analysis of local entropy revealed that the internal freedom of the molecules enhances the Soret effect, whereas their rigidity reduces it.

The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical limitations to their deployment. This paper sets out to dispute the prevailing notion that larger models necessarily lead to better performance. To this end, the study assesses the capabilities of four efficient transformer-based models – E-T5m, Peformer, CompactBERT, and ElasticEmbedding – in the context of Automated Essay Scoring, using a large dataset from the GE3 Challenge. Surprisingly, the analysis reveals that the existing top-performing model, E-T5m, can be surpassed by the other models, which demonstrate improved efficiency in terms of both computational performance and model parameter reduction.

One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on suppressing false positives in target domains using unsupervised methods.  To address this challenge, we transform the object detection task into a ranking task among positive and negative boxes, turning false positive suppression into an efficient box re-ranking problem without the need for manual annotation.  A novel ranking loss is introduced with a box alignment operator that effectively matches false positive boxes with their correct negative counterparts.  A cascaded network architecture is proposed with a main detector producing an initial set of boxes, which are then ranked and filtered through an auxiliary detector.  Our approach is evaluated across three benchmark datasets for pedestrian detection and delivers superior results with a minimal 1% loss in accuracy but significant 84.0% suppression of false positives compared to a standard domain adaptive detector.  Our method's source code is available at https://github.com/wheresthefish/box_re_ranking.

This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions like background noise, echo effects, and microphone distortion. A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one transforms audio in a specific representation called the mel-spectrogram into a new, more desirable format, and another converts synthetically created mel-spectrograms into high-quality audio waves that are perceptually natural-sounding. Experimental results indicate that our method effectively improves the audio quality by achieving a 5dB increase in the Signal to Noise Ratio metric and surpassing a competing method in the Mean Opinion Score by 0.1 on a 1-5 scale.

Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws where the point of release occurs early, in contrast to late releases. Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, points of release occurring late are often perceived as errors, whereas early releases tend to appear more authentic. These findings suggest that the dynamics and type of throw significantly influence the point at which a release point becomes apparent to observers. Moreover, variations in the point of release significantly affect the perceived force exerted in a throwing motion, thereby highlighting its relevance to realistic and convincing computer-generated animations of throwing actions.

To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2DRNN has been designed, which utilizes a tree-structured RNN has the top-level model. This type of model directly translates source text to a syntactically complete tree structure, enabling explicit logic during translation, and thus allows various optimization objectives to be easily incorporated into the training process. Furthermore, existing NMT models can be transformed into syntax-based models with minimal additional processing required. The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture is supported by experimental findings demonstrating its ability to meet both state-of-the-art translation quality and rigorous evaluation standards for machine translation and parsing.

The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse structures and energy patterns found at ice-grain surface binding sites. We developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) to store and distribute binding energy data for interstellar ice grain sites, obtained through extensive calculations using density functional theory-based interactions. Our platform provides access to a wide range of binding energy values for water, ammonia, methanol, formic acid, hydrogen oxide molecules, and other complex compounds, including polyatomic molecules and radicals. This study presents BEEP's first release, featuring binding energy data for July 2020, which serves as a resource for the astrochemical community, allowing researchers to compare existing binding energy values and guide future experimental and theoretical research directions in this field.

A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is studied, where a theoretical model of the process is developed and its distribution, characterized by four parameters, along with its limiting distribution, is analytically determined. Based on this model, a novel method for estimating the probability of a multiplicative stochastic process being less than a certain value at a particular time and having a minimum value at an earlier time is established. This method can be applied to real-world phenomena that involve growth, such as financial markets, where the multiplicative stochastic process represents trends and the minimum value represents losses. By assuming four parameters of the process's distribution, the model can accurately simulate various types of phenomena, including linear, nonlinear, power-law behaviors. Furthermore, the model's ability to estimate probabilities makes it applicable to practical problems, such as determining the probability of a company going bankrupt or the likelihood of a market dropping below a certain value.

We offer novel methods for approximating the expectation value of a quantum state with respect to a targeted Hamiltonian, primarily based on random unitary circuits of modest depth. The outcome of such a circuit can be viewed as a quantum shadow, a partial trace that approximates the state's Hamiltonian expectation value. The performance of our circuits is evaluated against standard reference circuits and several notable prior approaches, including random Pauli circuits, the linear combination of unitary operators, and the Zest protocol. While our results primarily focus on two-qubit circuits, we also examine single-qubit and multi-qubit variants, which are comparably efficient. The underlying reason for the success of these circuits is linked to their similarity in trace norms to the target state, thereby justifying their effectiveness in estimating Hamiltonian expectations.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ on a vertical line in a complex plane and its relation to polynomial and non-polynomial models of scattering. They managed to bypass a common restriction to $|k|$ being small and instead proved a new estimate which remains valid indefinitely. It becomes clear that for this result the behavior of the solution depends on whether $k$ is real or complex. Further investigation into this dependence is promised in a follow-up study where the authors will analyze particular examples of this dependence.

The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the need to preserve the original class label. In order to overcome this constraint, we propose a concept called sibylvariance, which refers to the use of data transforms that can vary class labels and lead to greater diversity in input data. To this end, we provide a comprehensive framework that encompasses two types of data transforms, SIB: (1) one form involves converting discrete categories into numerical values, (2) another form involves mapping input data to different classes while maintaining the original class label. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of these transforms on seven datasets and discover that the SIB form is capable of delivering a notable increase in diversity with minimal impact on model accuracy, outperforming traditional data transforms in the process. In addition, the proposed framework allows for the seamless integration of multiple data transforms and automated hyperparameter tuning, thus providing a versatile and adaptable framework for the efficient conversion of class labels.

Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. By utilizing regularizers and structured optimization techniques, we derive theoretical guarantees, demonstrating the sample efficiency of our methods and offering a new perspective on the theoretical underpinnings of meta-learning.

Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining eight languages in the process. Notably, it's discovered that distillation-based model performance variability heavily depends on several factors, such as whether ground truth labels are available, the learning strategy, and the level of supervision. To address these issues, we propose a novel training approach based on Quantization by Example, offering improved performance and a greater degree of control over its operation. Ultimately, we find that distillation is too fragile to reliably guarantee success in compressing MT models, whereas Quantization by Example, on the other hand, demonstrates greater consistency and is more effective in producing accurate translations for languages with limited training data.

The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted as ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted as pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities have been discovered, disproving a previous conjecture. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in certain cases and show that the Lagrangian density of a specific 3-uniform graph is sqrt(3)/3, resulting in an irrational Turan density, which answers an open question posed by Baber and Talbot.

The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms for identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering and annotating training data. To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labelled data in chest X-ray pneumonia detection through semantic segmentation. For a fair comparison, we employed a standard architecture for this task and trained it on subsets of a large dataset annotated by medical professionals, while also examining the effect of varying the quantity of labelled data available. Additionally, we evaluated the effectiveness of combining image augmentation methods in improving the model's performance when limited labelled data is used.

Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions according to the desired style and level of detail. This paper proposes a unified image captioning model that excels in both automatic and user-directed caption generation. Our model incorporates a prompt conditioning module that enables fine-grained control over caption attributes such as tone, verbosity, and descriptive quality. Additionally, the model can automatically adapt to diverse captioning domains with minimal labeled data in each domain, using a shared image feature extractor and adaptively combining pre-trained image and language models. Experiment results demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing methods in both automated and prompt-based captioning tasks.

As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causality and default utility. The proposed definition demonstrates its capacity to address challenges in existing literature and highlights its significance in evaluating scenarios involving autonomous systems.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an innovative open-source library that bridges the gap between Cognitive Toolkit and Apache Spark by introducing Java bindings and new components. The integration with OpenCV and the development of automated PySpark wrapper generation tool expands the capabilities of Spark's ecosystem. The MMLSpark library is accompanied by an extensive collection of tools and features. To demonstrate the potential of this collaboration, we develop a full-scale solution for automatically classifying Snow Leopards using camera trap images and apply it to aid the conservation efforts of the Snow Leopard Trust.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. To address this, a single model approach known as Speech Translation has made significant advancements but faces its own limitations when encountering unfamiliar spoken words, vocabulary gaps, and grammatical nuances. To overcome these challenges, we examine the feasibility of employing a multitask learning framework that integrates speech recognition and machine translation within a unified model. Our proposed model achieves this goal by optimizing the model's parameters via a self-supervised speech task and leveraging a large, publicly accessible dataset. As a result, it achieves impressive zero-shot performance by learning to recognize spoken words based on the listening human's representation of language and translating it into another language. To evaluate its performance, we conducted extensive testing on six prominent datasets. When comparing our findings to the state-of-the-art single-model Speech Translation approaches, our proposed model exhibits remarkably lower decoding overhead while delivering more accurate translations, especially on complex, real-world dialogues and unfamiliar spoken words.

This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a nonlinear balance condition. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels between the interior and boundary of the domain.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, where individual behaviors tend to dominate aggregate consumption profiles. Peak power demand during peak hours has a significant impact on the low voltage network, so accurately predicting these peaks is crucial for real-time distribution operations. This study examines the potential benefits of fusing the predictions of model ensembles in the context of probabilistic load forecasting, particularly for peak power demands, and showcases the importance of predictive model fusion by highlighting the variability of predictions and actual outcomes, and comparing them to historical records. The analysis is grounded in data from over 140,000 Danish consumers across five regions, and suggests that the best predictions are achieved by combining the forecasts of models that consider both weather and time-of-week factors. The results also indicate that the predictions are challenging during periods of variable weather and weekends, and that consumers' daily peak power demands exhibit considerable diversity. Overall, the findings emphasize the importance of using model ensemble forecasting for both peak and total power demands, although the forecasts may be less accurate for peak hours on Saturdays.

The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting AI performance, primarily due to limited data and insufficient resources. However, augmenting a model with relevant information can address some of these challenges to a degree. The difficulty in effectively integrating knowledge lies in the multiple forms of knowledge representation involved. This paper aims to provide an overview of various knowledge integration approaches and their effectiveness in machine learning applications.

Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite considerable advancements. The issue often arises due to annotation biases affecting traditional supervised segmentation techniques, which rely on detailed boundary markings. To resolve these issues and minimize labeling expenses, we introduce an innovative framework that utilizes image-level labels, thereby facilitating unbiased lesion detection and segmentation, as well as enhancing data-driven COVID-19 detection. This framework consists of two core components: a lesion detection model and an image-level classification network. The detection model uses the collected boundary data to correct any BiLM errors and detect relevant lesions, and its output is concurrently utilized to update the classification network. Notably, our proposal bypasses the necessity for pixel-level annotations, and through experiments, we have demonstrated superior performance in lesion detection, segmentation, and COVID-19 diagnosis compared to the current state-of-the-art methods.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgery planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth understanding of vertebrae anatomy to produce optimal results. By applying a series of preprocessing steps (including 3D filter and data-driven techniques to remove background noise and enhance vertebrae visibility), this method prepares a optimized starting point for the optimization algorithm. Subsequently, an optimization routine identifies the vertebrae by applying a specific cost function, while an anatomically-informed algorithm detects their center, following which, their 3D models can be reconstructed. Comprehensive testing across a large dataset of 85 CT scans with various spine pathologies indicates that our proposed approach outperforms existing methods and demonstrates particular efficacy in complicated imaging conditions.

Our theory explores the behavior of electron collisions with a strong repulsive barrier in a contained environment. Within an extremely high level of electron interaction with the surrounding electromagnetic field, temporary variations in the field energy lead to a steady state formation of an entwined state confined at the center of the barrier. As an incoming electron resonates with this confined state, it may temporarily attach to the entwined state through a virtual process. According to our calculation, a steady state confinement of milliseconds can occur when the gap between the entwined state and a nearby energy level is small. This steady state confinement is predicted to withstand a wide array of conditions including extreme temperatures and light-matter coupling levels. Conversely, when conditions prevent the formation of the entwined state, temporary variations in the electron interaction lead to a transient state confinement of short duration. Experiments utilizing a gold nanoparticle within a high-speed electron microscope have successfully detected both steady state confinement and entwined state destruction.

In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller's design. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, instead directly teaching model-free controllers to the actual robot. Initially, gaits are generated using central pattern generators with adjustable parameters. Then, the controller's parameters are fine-tuned through in-depth expert guidance to optimize its performance. We test this approach on a real-time quadruped robot named elasticbot equipped with series elastic actuators. Our study successfully demonstrates highly mobile and resilient controllers developed using this approach. These results exemplify a pioneering approach to developing spring-muscle-based controllers.

We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with minimal deviation in Hilbert-Schmidt distance. Our algorithm's performance is initially tested with GHZ states composed of up to seven qubits via simulations that utilize state vectors and random measurements. We also use numerical methods to determine the closest separable k-party states for up to ten qubits across various numbers of parties. Additionally, we outline a potential protocol for implementing VSV on current quantum devices and suggest that verifying separability serves as a novel test for quantum reliability.

A well-documented phenomenon, microtearing modes, occurs due to the electron temperature gradient in a plasma and causes fine-scale magnetic reconnections and the formation of magnetic islands. Prior research in a slab geometry setting showed that the drive mechanism requires collisions, but our simulations show that in the absence of collisions, there is still a small-scale, electron-driven tearing instability that exists. Detailed studies reveal that these modes are driven by electron temperature gradients but are influenced by electron finite radius effects and have properties that set them apart from larger-scale modes. Interestingly, these modes cause minimal disruption to the magnetic field, have a unique structure, and have low-frequency responses. What's more, these modes cause the electrons to concentrate in certain areas, creating richer, complex electron distributions that could aid in understanding various astrophysical phenomena.

A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only by image content, but also by image attributes as well. However, instances of fashion images with varied backgrounds and orientations are plentiful, resulting in the need to develop a robust approach that accounts for background and pose variations. This involves retrieving and searching images in a standardized format, specifically resized and stripped of backgrounds. Our method begins by defining fashion instance-level attribute manipulation, an innovative method that translates changes in attributes to corresponding image manipulations. It automatically alters raw images into the desired attributes while accounting for variations in background and pose, through learning a weighted average of images with varying backgrounds and poses related to a query image. These manipulated images are then automatically stripped of their backgrounds, represented in a standardized pose, and resized to a set height, thereby facilitating consistent search conditions. Furthermore, the method incorporates a ranking algorithm to select the most effective transformations from multiple possibilities, thereby presenting a superior approach to instance-level image retrieval.

The $\R$-optimal solution for the underdetermined equation $Ax=y$ where $A$ is a bounded linear operator mapping a Banach space to a Hilbert space, and $\R$ is a strongly convex function defined in that space, is considered for cases of incomplete data and noisy input. A dual gradient approach, though suffering from semi-convergence, can approximate the sought-after solution. Due to its underdetermined nature, the method requires an optimal stopping time, for which three rules – a priori choice, the discrepancy principle, and an adapted heuristic principle – are considered along with convergence and convergence rates results for the first two. Convergence results for the adapted principle are shown for specific conditions.

Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of each sub-aperture image with predefined offsets, making the process intricate and labor-intensive. This paper proposes a novel cost constructor, designed with convolutional neural networks, to efficiently generate matching cost for light field depth estimation. Our constructor, leveraging specifically engineered dilation rates, replicates the traditional offset-shifting method, thus enhancing the off-the-shelf status of the proposed pipeline. Our experimental results thoroughly validate the proposed constructor's performance superiority in multiple benchmark tests. Furthermore, we have successfully demonstrated the proposed pipeline's outstanding performance in light field depth estimation by achieving significant gains over state-of-the-art approaches, with training and inference times reduced by 87% and 13%, respectively.

This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a range of solutions for the reduced equations, resulting in a comprehensive set of solutions for both classical and nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations. Several solutions are illustrated through asymptotic analysis and colored density plots. Furthermore, this work outlines a step-by-step approach for utilizing the bilinear method to solve integrable partial differential equations, and serves as a case study for equation pairs of the form $m_t + (q \cdot \partial_x) m = Q(m)$, in the absence of constraints.

Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This action principle can be derived within double field theory (DFT), which provides a well-established framework for describing non-Riemannian gravity. DFT has been shown to be compatible with the proposed non-Riemannian gravity actions, which have been successfully derived for various types of these actions. We examine whether these actions describe the expected features of non-Riemannian gravity, including a system with a T^4 foliation and a black hole solution.

To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it's essential to optimize its performance. The increasing use of high-bandwidth applications like online gaming, streaming, and virtual reality services require efficient network management. To address this, it's crucial to utilize available network resources effectively by allowing devices to associate with the most suitable access points. This can be achieved through the AP/Extender selection mechanism, where a device chooses an AP or Extender based on the available connection options. However, in home WiFi networks, this can lead to interference between nearby WiFi networks, causing signal loss and decreased performance. To mitigate this, a new AP/Extender selection mechanism is proposed, utilizing IEEE 802.11k/v standards to enable fast handoffs and channel load load indication. This allows STAs to proactively select and hand off to a nearby network with better signal quality or load performance. To facilitate this, a new management object is introduced, allowing load performance to be evaluated and handoff decisions made. This enables faster and more efficient network adjustments, optimizing overall performance. By utilizing these standards, this mechanism can seamlessly integrate with existing home WiFi networks, enhancing its performance. Our test results confirm that this mechanism can reduce video stutters and average round trip times by 64.86% and 5.06%, respectively.
